newsitem.title: USA: Low U.S. soy stocks shut off forward soymeal sales.
newsitem.headline: Low U.S. soy stocks shut off forward soymeal sales.

text.p: Uncertainty over the availability of U.S. soybean supplies this summer has decreased the number of forward deals struck between end-users and soy crushers, soymeal dealers said.

"Usually people will offer April/September coverage as a package, but people are a little more reluctant to go past July this year because of (low) bean supplies," one southeastern soy processor said.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture forecast soybean 1997/98 ending stocks at 125 million bushels, which is the lowest since 1976, according to USDA data.

The record-low stocks have generated processor concerns over the availability of soybeans during the summer months. As a result, most offers for summer delivery soymeal include a steep premium, brokers said.
"When the processors do put a price on forward delivery, it's going to cost the end-user because the processor doesn't know what his beans are going to cost," one broker said.
Soymeal basis offers for July delivery in Illinois are quoted at approximately $11.00 or $12.00 per ton over CBOT July futures and delivery for August is $15.00 per ton over, dealers said.
In contrast, soymeal for spot delivery in Illinois was offered at $5.00 per ton on Tuesday, basis May futures, cash sources said.
But the summer delivery premiums and perceptions that that market will move lower as U.S. farmers plant more acres to soybeans this year have kept most end-users out of forward markets, dealers said.
"In past years, we have seen people willing to do summer meal," said a southeastern broker. "But we aren't seeing a lot of September/August meal trading right now."
One dealer who supplies poultry and hog producers in the southeast with soymeal estimated total summer soymeal coverage was only about 50 percent, which is well below normal levels, he said.
The southeastern corn market does not favor forward sales right now either, one railcar corn merchandiser said.
"I can only speak for the rail corn markets, but there's no incentive to go out and own forward basis," said the dealer. "The market is not paying you to own forward basis."
The dealer cautioned however, that market conditions could change quickly and forward sales could pick up speed.
"The market is going to tell people what to do," he said. "It could change at any moment."
